lead: A hot-wire anemometer measures flow speed by heating a fine wire and noting how much current is needed to keep it hot. A resistance hygrometer measures humidity by letting a moist film change its electrical resistance. Both are resistance devices: one reads velocity, the other reads water vapour. You meet them in air ducts, wind tunnels, engine intakes, textile mills, cold stores and weather stations.
prereq: You need RTDs and thermistors for resistance against temperature, and the first-order thermal lag from dynamic characteristics.

blocks.text: A hot-wire probe is a platinum or tungsten wire a few micrometres across and a few millimetres long, mounted on two prongs. A current I heats it above the flow temperature Ta. The flow removes heat by convection. At steady state the electrical power equals the heat carried away:

blocks.where: I is heating current in A; R<sub>w</sub> is wire resistance in Ω; h is the convective heat-transfer coefficient in W/(m²·K); A is wire surface area in m²; T<sub>w</sub> is wire temperature in K; T<sub>a</sub> is flow temperature in K.

blocks.text: King's law relates h to flow speed u:

blocks.where: h is the convective heat-transfer coefficient; u is flow speed in m/s; a and b are constants found by calibration.

blocks.text: The square-root form comes from boundary-layer heat transfer over a cylinder. Combine it with the resistance–temperature relation of the RTD, Rw = R0[1 + α(Tw − T0)], and the bridge output E follows:

blocks.where: E is output voltage in V; A and B are calibration constants; u is flow speed in m/s; n is near 0.5.

blocks.text: The instrument is linear only in E² against √u. Plotting E against u gives a curve, not a straight line.

In constant-current mode the heating current is fixed. When flow rises the wire cools, R<sub>w</sub> falls, and the voltage across it drops. The bridge unbalance is the output. This mode is simple but slow: the wire must heat or cool, and its thermal lag is first order.

In constant-temperature mode a feedback amplifier holds R<sub>w</sub>, and therefore T<sub>w</sub>, fixed. Flow tries to cool the wire; the bridge error makes the amplifier drive more current. That drive current, read as a voltage E, is the output. This mode is faster and less sensitive to ambient temperature, but needs a stable feedback loop.

items: A second unheated cold wire measures T<sub>a</sub> for temperature compensation.
Calibration uses known velocities in a wind tunnel or a calibrated nozzle.
A single wire senses speed normal to it; a split-film or three-wire probe gives direction.
Hot-film probes with a thin metallic film on a glass or quartz substrate work in liquids.
Uses include duct and wind-tunnel velocity, engine intake flow and turbulence; in medicine, heated-film flow sensors measure breathing flow in ventilators and spirometers.

blocks.text: Relative humidity (RH) is the ratio of water vapour present to the saturation amount at the same temperature, usually expressed as a percentage. It is not absolute humidity, which is the mass of water vapour per unit volume, and not dew point, the temperature at which air becomes saturated.

A resistance hygrometer has a hygroscopic film between two electrodes: a conductive polymer, a treated ceramic, or a lithium-chloride layer. Water uptake raises ionic conduction, so resistance falls as RH rises. Over a limited range the fall is roughly log-linear, about one decade per 30 % RH.

Typical range is 10 % to 90 % RH, accuracy a few percent RH and response from seconds to minutes; contamination and temperature changes cause drift, so the film must be kept clean and calibrated. Uses: textile mills, cold stores, weather stations and grain storage, and in hospitals the humidity of neonatal incubators and of the warmed gas a ventilator delivers. Capacitive humidity sensors come with the chemical sensors.

figure.caption: Left: flow cools the heated wire, the bridge unbalances, and the amplifier raises the bridge voltage E until the wire is back at its set resistance; E is the reading. Right: the worked example’s King’s law is a straight line of E² against √u: 3.16 V at 9 m/s, and 3.46 V means 15.9 m/s.

spec.aria: Left: a Wheatstone bridge with the hot wire in one arm and an amplifier whose output feeds the top of the bridge, with flow arrows cooling the wire. Right: a straight line of E squared against the square root of speed starting at 4 volts squared, with points at 9 metres per second giving 3.16 volts and at 15.9 metres per second giving 3.46 volts.

examples.question: A constant-temperature hot-wire anemometer follows E² = A + B√u with A = 4 V² and B = 2 V²/(m/s)<sup>0.5</sup>. (a) Find E at u = 9 m/s. (b) Find u when E = 3.46 V. (c) A resistive hygrometer reads 1 MΩ at 30 % RH and 100 kΩ at 60 % RH. Using a log-linear law, find R at 45 % RH.
steps: (c) From 30 % to 60 % RH the resistance falls one decade, 1 MΩ to 100 kΩ, so log R falls 1/30 decade per %RH. At 45 % RH, 15 % above 30 %, R = 1 MΩ × 10<sup>−15/30</sup> = 1 MΩ/√10 = 316.2 kΩ.
Note in (a) and (b): u rose 1.77 times (9 to 15.9 m/s) while E rose only 9.5 % (3.16 to 3.46 V); the square-root law compresses high speeds, so resolution is poorest there.

traps: Plotting E against u and expecting a straight line. The calibration is linear only in E² against √u.
Mixing up relative humidity and absolute humidity. RH changes with temperature even when the water vapour content stays the same.
Forgetting temperature compensation on a hot wire. The wire also responds to T<sub>a</sub>, so a cold wire or a compensated bridge is needed.
Using inconsistent units in King's law. B carries units of V²/(m s⁻¹)<sup>0.5</sup> when u is in m/s.
Assuming a resistive hygrometer is linear in RH. It is roughly log-linear, about one decade per 30 % RH.

quiz.q: State King's law for a hot-wire anemometer and name each symbol.
quiz.a: h = a + b·u<sup>0.5</sup>, where h is the convective heat-transfer coefficient, u is flow speed, and a and b are calibration constants.

quiz.q: Why does a constant-temperature hot-wire anemometer respond faster than a constant-current one?
quiz.a: In constant-temperature mode feedback holds the wire temperature fixed, so the drive current changes at once. In constant-current mode the wire itself must heat or cool, and its first-order thermal lag slows the output.

quiz.q: A hot-wire follows E² = 6 + 3√u with E in V and u in m/s. Find u when E = 6 V.
A resistive hygrometer reads 2 MΩ at 20 % RH and 200 kΩ at 50 % RH. Find its sensitivity in decades per %RH and predict R at 35 % RH.
quiz.a: One decade in 30 % RH, so 1/30 ≈ 0.033 decade per %RH. At 35 % RH, 15 % above 20 %, the fall is half a decade: R = 2 MΩ × 10<sup>−0.5</sup> = 632 kΩ.
Relative humidity is the ratio of the water vapour present to the saturation amount at the same temperature, expressed as a percentage.

quiz.q: Why can a resistive hygrometer reading change with temperature even when absolute humidity is constant?
quiz.a: The film responds to relative humidity. When temperature changes, the saturation vapour pressure changes, so RH changes even if the absolute water vapour content is fixed.

quiz.q: At 40 % RH a sensor reads 500 kΩ. Assuming one decade per 30 % RH, find R at 70 % RH.
quiz.a: The change is 30 % RH, exactly one decade. Resistance falls by a factor of 10, so R = 50 kΩ.

quiz.q: Give two reasons a hot-wire anemometer may read low in dusty engine intake air and one remedy.
quiz.a: Dust deposits on the wire change its surface area and add an insulating layer, so heat transfer calibration drifts; dirt can also change the effective probe geometry. Remedy: filter the sample, clean the probe, and recalibrate or use a protected hot-film probe.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern instruments use micromachined hot-film bridges on silicon, with on-chip temperature sensors and digital linearisation. Researchers use hot-wire arrays to measure turbulence spectra and wall shear stress. Humidity sensing has moved to capacitive polymer and MEMS sensors, but resistive films remain common in cheap hygrostats. Search for 'constant-temperature anemometer bridge', 'hot-film shear stress sensor' and 'resistive humidity sensor drift'.
